title: HAMLET: Switch Your Vision-Language-Action Model into a History-Aware Policy
claim: Tasks needing memory of past context cannot be solved from the current observation alone, and ours succeeds where baselines fail.
layout: 2 panels: left task filmstrips with callouts, right bar charts; highlighted ours
description: Two-part figure. Panel (a), "History-dependent Long-horizon Tasks", has two rows of five real-world robot camera frames linked by orange arrows. Each row has a speech-bubble instruction at top: "Cover the cube with the nearest cup, then stack the other cup on top of it" (upper) and "Swap the two cubes, starting with the blue one" (lower). Blue-bordered frames with blue captions ("The cube is under the blue cup…", "The blue cube was on the right…") show the memory the robot needs. Red-bordered frames with red captions ("Wait, where is the cube?", "Wait, which cube to grasp next?") mark the moment the current view is ambiguous. Panel (b), "Success Rates", has two horizontal stacked bar charts, one per task, comparing GR00T N1.5 (yellow), + Multi-frame (orange) and + HAMLET (ours, blue). Each bar is split into full and partial success. A red dashed box highlights the ours rows. The eye goes first to the photo strips with the red and blue callouts.
caption: Examples of history-dependent long-horizon tasks. (a) Real-world tasks that involve cases such as object occlusion (upper) or multi-step reasoning (lower) are inherently non-Markovian: proper actions cannot be determined from the current observation alone. (b) Success rates on these tasks show that HAMLET significantly outperforms both GR00T N1.5 and the na¨ıve multi-frame baseline, demonstrating its ability to leverage historical context for reliable long-horizon control.
abstract: Inherently, robotic manipulation tasks are history-dependent: leveraging past context could be beneficial. However, most existing Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have been designed without considering this aspect, i.e., they rely solely on the current observation, ignoring preceding context. In this paper, we propose HAMLET, a scalable framework to adapt VLAs to attend to the historical context during action prediction. Specifically, we introduce moment tokens that compactly encode perceptual information at each timestep. Their representations are initialized with time-contrastive learning, allowing them to better capture temporally distinctive aspects. Next, we employ a lightweight memory module that integrates the moment tokens across past timesteps into memory features, which are then leveraged for action prediction. Through empirical evaluation, we show that HAMLET successfully transforms a state-of-the-art VLA into a history-aware policy, especially demonstrating significant improvements on long-horizon tasks that require historical context. In particular, on top of GR00T N1.5, HAMLET achieves an average success rate of 76.4% on history-dependent real-world tasks, surpassing the baseline performance by 47.2%. Furthermore, HAMLET pushes prior art performance from 64.1% to 66.4% on RoboCasa Kitchen (100-demo setup) and from 95.6% to 97.7% on LIBERO, highlighting its effectiveness even under generic robot-manipulation benchmarks.
